Many said they had already spent their marketing budget, so I began approaching them earlier in the quarter, and I prepared a short one-page proposal showing what they would get. That improved my results. I learnt that a no is often about timing or the way you ask, not about you. In insurance sales I expect many rejections, and I plan to treat each one as information, thank the person politely, and move on to the next call.

samples.who: Experienced (bank sales officer moving to fintech sales)
samples.answer: In my current role selling credit cards and personal loans, I make about [number] calls a day, and most say no. What helps me is focusing on what I control: the number of calls, the quality of my conversation and follow-ups. After a tough day I review my notes and identify one thing to change tomorrow. I also keep a simple record of customers who said 'not now', because some of them come back months later when their needs change. I never argue with a customer who refuses, since that only damages future chances.

mistakes: Saying rejection does not affect you at all, which sounds unrealistic.
Describing pressuring the customer until they agree.
Blaming customers or the product for every rejection.
Giving a theoretical answer with no example.
follow_ups: What would you do after ten rejections in a row?
How do you stay motivated in a slow month?
Tell me about a time you turned a no into a yes.
How many calls do you think you can make in a day?
faqs: What if I have no sales experience?

Use any situation where you asked for something and were refused: sponsorships, internship applications, fund-raising, selling at a college stall, or even exam failures you bounced back from. Show what you learnt and how you kept going.
Should I mention mental health or stress?

You can briefly mention healthy habits that help you reset, such as exercise or talking to a mentor. Keep the focus on resilience and learning. Interviewers want to see that you have practical ways to handle pressure.

items.question: Are you comfortable working with sales targets?
items.title: Are You Comfortable With Sales Targets? Interview Answer
items.description: Answer the targets question in insurance, bank and fintech sales interviews with honesty, a plan and an ethical line. Sample answers included.
items.why_asked: Targets are central to sales roles in insurance, bank cross-selling, credit cards, loans and fintech. Interviewers ask this to see if you understand that, and to weed out people who will quit after the first difficult month. A simple 'yes' is not enough. They want to know how you break a target into daily activity, how you handle pressure, and whether you understand that targets must be met ethically, without mis-selling. Candidates who talk about planning, discipline and customer focus, rather than just enthusiasm, come across as dependable.
how_to_answer: Give a clear yes and show that you understand targets are a normal, fair way to measure performance in sales.
Explain how you break a monthly target into weekly and daily activities, such as calls, meetings and proposals.
Share an example of working toward a numerical goal, from a past job, internship or college role.
Mention how you handle a slow period, such as analysing your pipeline, asking for help, or focusing on existing customers.
Draw an ethical line: you will meet targets by finding the right customers, not by mis-selling or hiding product terms.

samples.answer: Yes, I am comfortable. I think targets give clarity on what is expected. When I get a monthly target, I would work backwards. For example, if I need 20 savings accounts and I know roughly one in five meetings converts, I need around 100 good conversations, which is about five a day. Breaking it down that way makes it manageable. During my internship at [company] I had a target of [number] survey responses or leads and I tracked my progress daily in a sheet. I would also be honest with customers. I would rather meet my target with the right customers than get complaints later.

samples.who: Experienced (insurance advisor moving to a bancassurance role)
samples.answer: I have worked with monthly and quarterly targets for [number] years. Some months I exceeded them, and a few times I fell short. What I learnt is that the pipeline matters more than the last week. I keep at least two to three times my target in active prospects and I follow up consistently. In the last week of a quarter there is always pressure to push any policy to anyone; I avoid that, because a policy that lapses or gets cancelled in the free-look period hurts both the customer and the company.

mistakes: Saying you can achieve any target without knowing what it is.
Admitting you dislike targets or find them unfair.
Describing meeting targets by pushing unsuitable products.
Having no method for planning your activity.
follow_ups: What will you do if you miss your target for two months?
How would you plan your first month here?
What is the free-look period in insurance?
What if your target seems unrealistic?
faqs: Should I ask about the target size in the interview?

Yes, it is reasonable to ask how targets are set, how performance is reviewed and what support new joiners get. Ask in a curious, positive way near the end of the interview rather than as a condition.
What if I have never had a target before?

Use any numerical goal you worked toward, such as fund-raising, recruiting members for a club, selling event tickets or a study plan. Show how you planned, tracked and adjusted. That demonstrates the habit interviewers want.

items.question: How would you approach a cold call to a customer who has never heard of us?
items.title: How Do You Approach Cold Calling? Sales Interview Answer
items.description: Cold-calling interview question for insurance, credit card, loan and fintech roles: opening line, permission, needs questions, compliance and follow-up.
items.why_asked: Telesales and field sales in insurance, credit cards, personal loans and fintech often begin with cold calls. Interviewers want to know if you can open a conversation politely, earn a minute of attention, ask good questions and handle a quick no without being rude. They also check whether you know the rules: calling only permitted numbers, respecting Do Not Disturb preferences under TRAI rules, identifying yourself and your company clearly, and never misrepresenting the product. Many interviews include a live mock call, so a structured approach you can actually deliver is better than theory.
how_to_answer: Prepare before calling: know who the customer is likely to be, the one problem your product solves, and what you want from the call, such as a meeting.
Open with your name, company and reason in one or two sentences, then ask permission to continue.
Ask one or two short questions to understand the customer's situation, rather than reading a long script.
Offer a specific next step, such as sending details on WhatsApp or a short meeting, and confirm a time.
Respect a no politely, follow DND and consent rules, and log the call outcome for follow-up.

samples.who: Fresher (fintech telesales interview, live mock call)
samples.answer: Good afternoon, am I speaking with Mr Sharma? My name is [name] and I am calling from [company], a [payments or lending] app. I will take just one minute; is this a good time? ... Thank you. We help small shop owners accept digital payments and get settlements the next morning. May I ask, do you currently accept UPI at your shop? ... And do you sometimes face delays in getting the money in your account? ... I understand. Many shop owners in your area use our QR with a [settlement feature]. If it is convenient, I can send you the details on WhatsApp and our field executive can visit on Thursday at 11. Would that work?

samples.who: Experienced (credit card sales moving to insurance telesales)
samples.answer: I believe the first ten seconds decide the call. I always state my name, company and purpose clearly, because customers get many fraud calls and they need to know who I am. I then ask permission. If they say they are busy, I ask for a better time instead of continuing. My goal is not to sell on the first call but to qualify and set a next step. I keep notes in the CRM on what they said, so the next call feels personal. I also never pressure anyone who says they are not interested, and I check DND status as per our process.

mistakes: Reading a long script without pausing for the customer.
Not identifying yourself and your company clearly.
Pushing ahead when the customer says they are busy.
Making exaggerated claims like 'zero charges forever' without being sure.
Ignoring DND preferences and consent requirements.
follow_ups: The customer says 'I am not interested'. What next?
How many calls can you make in a day?
What is the DND registry?
How do you sound different from fraud callers?
faqs: What is the DND registry and why does it matter?

The National Customer Preference Register lets telecom subscribers block unsolicited commercial calls and messages in chosen categories. Companies must follow TRAI rules on commercial communication. Mention that you would follow your company's compliance process on calling lists and consent.
How long should my opening be?
Ten to fifteen seconds: name, company, reason and a permission question. Customers decide quickly whether to listen. A short, respectful opening earns more time than a long pitch delivered too fast.

items.question: How would you cross-sell to an existing customer without being pushy?
items.title: How to Cross-Sell Ethically: Bank and Insurance Interviews
items.description: Answer the cross-selling question in bank, insurance and NBFC interviews by linking products to real needs, disclosing terms and never bundling by force.
items.why_asked: Cross-selling insurance, mutual funds, credit cards and loans to existing customers is a major revenue source for banks and NBFCs, and also a major source of complaints. Regulators have repeatedly warned against forced bundling, such as making insurance a condition for a loan when it is not required, or selling insurance to elderly depositors as FDs. Interviewers ask this to check both your selling skill and your ethics. They want to hear a needs-based approach, clear disclosure, respect for the customer's choice and an understanding of the difference between cross-selling and mis-selling.
how_to_answer: Explain that good cross-selling starts with the customer's life events and needs, such as a new home loan, a new child, or a large maturing deposit.
Show how you would ask questions and listen, instead of offering every product to every customer.
Describe clear disclosure: what the product is, its costs, lock-in and risks, and that it is optional.
Mention specific red lines, such as never tying an optional product to loan approval and never calling insurance a deposit.
Say you would take the customer's written consent, give time to decide, and respect a no.

samples.who: Fresher (bank PO or sales officer interview)
samples.answer: I would look for a real need first. Suppose a young couple has just taken a home loan from us. A natural question is, 'If something happens to one of you, how will the EMI be paid?' That opens a conversation about term insurance. I would explain the options, the premium and that it is completely optional, and that the loan does not depend on it. If they want time, I would give them the brochure and follow up. I would never tell a customer that the loan will be delayed without insurance, or describe a market-linked plan as a fixed deposit. If they say no, I note it and do not keep pushing.

In my last role I saw how cross-selling can go wrong, with senior citizens being sold long-term ULIPs instead of renewing their FDs. That led to complaints and refunds. My approach is to review the customer's profile and ask about their plans before suggesting anything. I disclose charges and lock-ins upfront and confirm their understanding by asking them to explain it back to me. I also make sure the product matches their age and income. My conversion rate is a little lower than some colleagues', but my persistency and complaint record are much better.

mistakes: Saying you would offer all products to every customer.
Linking an optional product to loan approval.
Describing insurance or market-linked products as deposits.
Ignoring the customer's age, income or existing coverage.
follow_ups: What is the difference between cross-selling and mis-selling?
What is the free-look period?
What is persistency in insurance?
What would you say if your manager asks you to bundle insurance with every loan?
faqs: Is it wrong to cross-sell?

No. Cross-selling is useful when a product genuinely meets a customer's need, and existing customers often prefer dealing with an institution they trust. It becomes mis-selling when the product does not suit the customer or terms are hidden or misrepresented.
What is persistency and why mention it?

Persistency measures how many policies are still being renewed after a period, such as 13 months. Low persistency often signals mis-selling. Mentioning it shows you understand that a sale is only good if the customer keeps the product because it suits them.

items.question: Sell me a term insurance policy.
items.title: Sell Me a Term Insurance Policy: Interview Role-Play Tips
items.description: Role-play for insurance and bancassurance interviews: sell term insurance by understanding dependants, cover need and objections, with honest disclosure.
items.why_asked: Insurance and bancassurance interviews often swap the pen for a real product. Term insurance is a favourite because it is simple, genuinely useful and frequently misunderstood. Interviewers check whether you can identify the need, estimate cover in a sensible way, explain features such as sum assured, policy term and exclusions, and handle common objections like 'I get nothing back if I survive'. They also watch for mis-selling signals, such as pushing return-of-premium variants without explanation, or making claims about claim settlement you cannot support.
how_to_answer: Begin with questions about dependants, income, loans and existing cover, since term insurance is about protecting people who depend on the buyer's income.
Explain the product simply: a fixed premium for a chosen term, and if the insured dies during that term, the nominee receives the sum assured.
Show a rough cover calculation, such as a multiple of annual income plus outstanding loans, while saying the exact need depends on the family's situation.
Handle the 'no maturity benefit' objection by comparing it to vehicle or health insurance, which also pay only on an event.
Mention honest disclosure: full and correct health information, exclusions, and checking the insurer's claim settlement data on IRDAI or the insurer's site.

samples.answer: Sir, can I ask, who depends on your income today? ... Your wife, two children and your parents. And do you have any loans? ... A home loan of about ₹30 lakh. If, God forbid, something happened to you, how would the EMI and the children's education be managed? ... That is exactly what term insurance is for. You pay a fixed yearly premium, and if anything happens to you during the policy term, your family gets a lump sum, say ₹1 crore, which can clear the loan and support them. You mentioned you get nothing back if you survive. That is true, just like your car insurance, but because there is no savings part, the premium is much lower than other life policies. The key is to disclose your health details fully so the claim is smooth. Shall we work out the right cover together?

I always begin with the family, not the product. For a 32-year-old salaried customer with a home loan, I calculate a rough cover based on income replacement and liabilities and show it on paper. I compare two or three term options on premium, term and riders like accidental death, and explain exclusions. When customers ask about return of premium versions, I explain clearly that the premium is much higher and they can compare that with buying pure term and investing the difference elsewhere. I let them decide. I also tell them to inform their nominee about the policy.

mistakes: Promising that every claim will be paid.
Advising the customer to hide health conditions or smoking to reduce premium.
Pushing return-of-premium or savings plans without explaining the cost difference.
Quoting a premium without knowing age, health and cover.
follow_ups: The customer says he already has a policy from his employer. What next?
What is a rider?
What is the claim settlement ratio, and is it the only thing to check?
Why is non-disclosure dangerous?
faqs: Should I quote claim settlement ratios in the role-play?

Only general guidance. Tell the customer that insurers publish claim settlement data and IRDAI's annual report has industry figures, and that they should check the latest numbers. Avoid quoting a specific insurer's ratio from memory.
How much cover should I suggest?

Interviewers want a reasoned approach, not a fixed rule. Mention income replacement for a number of years plus loans and major goals, minus existing cover and assets. Say the final figure depends on the family's needs and the insurer's underwriting.

items.question: Why do you want to work in sales?
items.title: Why Do You Want a Sales Job? Answers for Finance Sales
items.description: Answer 'Why sales?' for insurance, banking, NBFC and fintech sales roles with real motivation beyond incentives. Samples for freshers and switchers.
items.why_asked: Many candidates apply for sales roles because they are the most available jobs in financial services, not because they want to sell. Interviewers know this and ask the question to find people who will stay through the tough first months. They listen for genuine reasons: enjoying conversations, liking measurable results, wanting fast growth, or wanting to help customers make good decisions. Incentives are a fair reason but should not be the only one. The panel also checks whether you understand what the job involves, such as field travel, rejection, targets and paperwork.
how_to_answer: Give one or two genuine reasons with evidence, such as enjoying persuading people, liking clear targets, or past experiences in college events or a family business.
Show that you understand the job's realities: frequent rejection, monthly targets, field travel, repeated follow-ups and documentation.
Connect sales to the financial product you will sell, explaining why helping people with insurance, loans or investments interests you.
Mention earnings and incentive-linked growth honestly but briefly, as one motivation among several rather than the main one.
Close with how you see your sales career developing over a few years, such as moving to team leader or relationship manager.

samples.who: Fresher (BBA, applying for bank sales executive)
samples.answer: I have always enjoyed talking to people and convincing them. In college I handled sponsorships for our fest and got [number] sponsors, and I liked the challenge of turning a no into a yes. Sales is also one of the few jobs where your results are clear every month, and that motivates me. I chose financial products because they actually matter in people's lives; a good loan or insurance decision can help a family a lot. I know the job involves a lot of calls, rejection and field visits, and I am ready for that. The incentives are attractive too, but what I really want is to become someone customers trust and to grow into a relationship manager role.

samples.who: Career switcher (from back-office operations to insurance sales)
samples.answer: I have spent two years in operations processing policy documents, and I kept noticing that the customers who understood their policies well were the ones handled by good advisors. I want to be that person. Operations taught me product details and paperwork accuracy, which many new salespeople struggle with. I also want a role where my effort directly shows in my results. I understand there will be months with low numbers, but I am prepared to build slowly through referrals and service.

mistakes: Saying you applied because you could not find another job.
Talking only about incentives and money.
Describing yourself as 'a people person' with no evidence.
Underestimating the hard parts of the job.
follow_ups: What do you think is the hardest part of a sales job?
Sell me this product.
How much do you expect to earn through incentives?
Where do you see yourself in three years in sales?
faqs: Is it okay to say money motivates me?

Yes, sales is one of the few roles where earnings depend on performance, and interviewers know that. Just do not make it your only reason. Pair it with enjoying customer interaction and achieving clear goals.
I am an introvert. Can I still do well in sales?

Many successful salespeople are introverts who listen well and prepare thoroughly. You can mention that you are a good listener and organised with follow-ups. Interviewers value consistency and trust more than loudness.

items.question: What do you understand about the role of a relationship manager?
items.title: What Does a Relationship Manager Do? Interview Answer
items.description: Explain the relationship manager role in bank, wealth and NBFC interviews: portfolio, acquisition, service, cross-sell, compliance and client retention.
items.why_asked: Relationship manager is one of the most common titles in Indian banks, NBFCs, wealth firms and brokerages, and the role varies: branch banking RM, wealth RM, SME or business banking RM, or priority banking RM. Interviewers ask this to check whether you understand the job beyond 'handling clients'. They want to hear about managing a portfolio of customers, growing balances and relationships, cross-selling suitable products, ensuring service quality and complying with KYC and suitability rules. A specific answer shows you researched the role and will not be surprised by its sales component.
how_to_answer: Describe the core: an RM owns a portfolio of clients and is their main point of contact for banking or investment needs.
Explain the two sides, growing the relationship through deposits, investments and loans, and retaining clients through good service.
Mention typical metrics, such as portfolio size, new acquisitions, product penetration, client retention and complaint levels.
Include the compliance responsibilities too: periodic KYC updates, suitability checks, clear disclosure, and protecting client data.
Connect your answer to the specific type of RM role you applied for and the skills or experience you bring to it.

samples.who: Fresher (MBA, applying for branch banking RM)
samples.answer: A relationship manager is the main contact for a group of the bank's customers, usually those with higher balances. The RM's job is to understand each customer's needs, make sure their banking experience is smooth, and offer relevant products like fixed deposits, mutual funds, insurance or loans at the right time. RMs are measured on things like growth in the portfolio's balances, new clients, product holding and retention. Service is a big part, because a client who is unhappy will move money elsewhere. The RM also handles KYC updates and must make sure every product sold is suitable. I think my communication skills and my NISM V-A certification will help me build trust quickly.

samples.who: Experienced (sales officer moving to SME relationship manager)
samples.answer: For an SME RM, the client is a business, so the relationship covers current accounts, working capital, term loans, trade finance and the owner's personal banking. The RM coordinates with credit, operations and product teams, and is responsible for early warning signs like delayed payments or falling turnover. I have sold current accounts and business loans for [number] years, so I know many local businesses already. What I want to build is deeper relationship management, where I support a client's growth over years rather than one transaction.

mistakes: Describing the RM role as only customer service, ignoring sales.
Describing it as only sales, ignoring service and compliance.
Not knowing which type of RM role you applied for.
Using vague phrases like 'managing relationships' without specifics.
follow_ups: How would you handle a client who wants to move his money to another bank?
How many clients can one RM manage effectively?
What products would you offer a client with a large FD maturing?
How do you balance sales targets with client interests?
faqs: Is a relationship manager role a sales job?

Largely, yes. Most RM roles have targets for acquisition, balances and product sales. But unlike pure acquisition roles, RMs also handle service and retention for an existing portfolio. Understanding both sides is important in the interview.
What certifications help for RM roles?

For roles involving mutual funds, NISM Series V-A is commonly needed, and an IRDAI-mandated certification is needed for selling insurance. Some wealth roles prefer NISM X-A or CFP. Check the job description and your employer's requirements.

items.question: What will you do if you miss your monthly sales target?
items.title: What If You Miss Your Sales Target? Interview Answer
items.description: How to answer the missed target question in insurance, bank and fintech sales interviews: own it, analyse the pipeline, fix the plan, stay ethical.
items.why_asked: Every salesperson misses a target at some point. Interviewers ask this to see how you react: with excuses, panic, unethical shortcuts or a calm plan. They want to see ownership, the ability to analyse what went wrong, using data like calls, meetings and conversion rates, and a concrete recovery plan. They also want to know if you will communicate early with your manager rather than hiding the shortfall until month-end. Candidates who say 'I will never miss a target' sound naive, and those who blame the market or product sound like future problems.
how_to_answer: Accept that it can happen and take ownership instead of blaming leads, products or the market.
Explain how you would analyse the gap: activity levels, conversion at each stage, average ticket size and lost deals.
Describe a recovery plan, such as increasing quality meetings, re-contacting warm leads, or focusing on an underused segment.
Mention involving your manager early, asking for coaching or joint calls rather than hiding the problem.
State that you would not cut ethical corners, like mis-selling or pushing unsuitable products, to close the gap.

samples.answer: If I miss a target, I would first look at my own numbers honestly. Did I make enough calls and meetings? If my activity was fine but conversions were low, maybe my pitch or the customer segment was wrong. If activity was low, I need better planning. I would discuss this with my team leader early, not at the end of the month, and ask for feedback, maybe by having him join a few of my calls. Then I would set a clear plan for the next month, like adding [number] extra meetings a week and following up on all pending applications. I would not try to make up numbers by pushing cards to people who do not need them, because those lead to complaints and cancellations.

I missed my target twice last year. Both times, when I analysed it, I found my pipeline had dried up because I had stopped prospecting while closing a few large policies. Since then I spend a fixed hour every morning on new prospects, regardless of how busy I am with closures. I also look at renewals and service, because satisfied clients bring referrals. When I see I am likely to fall short by mid-month, I tell my manager and we agree on specific actions. That has kept me within reach of target even in slow months.

mistakes: Claiming you will never miss a target.
Blaming the product, leads or economy.
Saying you would push any product to anyone to make up numbers.
Not mentioning any analysis or plan.
follow_ups: What if you miss it three months in a row?
How do you track your pipeline?
What is a good conversion rate in your view?
How would you react if a colleague is meeting targets through mis-selling?
faqs: Should I admit I have missed targets before?

Yes, if it is true. Interviewers trust candidates who admit past shortfalls and explain what they changed. Pair the admission with the analysis and improvement that followed, so the story ends with learning and better results.
What is a sales pipeline?

A pipeline is the list of prospects at different stages: first contact, meeting, proposal, documentation and closure. Tracking it shows where deals get stuck and whether you have enough prospects to meet future targets.

items.question: How would you convince a kirana shop owner to start using our payment app or QR?
items.title: Convince a Shopkeeper to Use Your Payment App: Interview
items.description: Fintech field sales role-play: pitching a QR or payment app to a kirana store owner. Understand their worries about fees, settlement and fraud.
items.why_asked: Fintech companies, payment aggregators and banks hire large field sales teams to onboard merchants. This role-play tests whether you can sell to a busy small business owner who has little time and many suppliers asking for attention. Interviewers check whether you understand the merchant's real concerns: settlement speed, charges, sound box alerts, fraud, and the hassle of multiple QR codes. They also look for practical sales sense, like visiting at quiet hours, speaking the local language, and offering a quick setup. Honesty about charges and terms matters as much as persuasion.
how_to_answer: Mention timing and approach: visit during a quiet hour, greet respectfully, and speak in the shopkeeper's language.
Ask what he currently uses for payments and what problems he faces, such as fake payment screenshots, delayed settlement or customers without cash.
Link your product's features to those problems, such as instant payment alerts through a sound box, next-day settlement or a simple app dashboard.
Be transparent about any charges, rental or terms, and do not overpromise features you are not sure of.
Offer a quick, easy start, such as same-day KYC and QR setup, and a follow-up visit to make sure it works.

samples.answer: I would visit in the afternoon when the shop is less busy. I would greet him and ask, 'Bhaiya, do customers pay you through UPI these days?' Most say yes. Then I would ask if he has ever had a problem with fake payment screenshots or not hearing whether money came in when the shop is crowded. That is where our sound box helps; it announces every payment aloud. I would show him the app and how he can see the day's total at closing time. I would clearly tell him about any rental or charges so there is no surprise later. If he agrees, I can complete his KYC on the spot and set up the QR. I would come back in a week to check it is working.

samples.who: Experienced (FMCG distributor sales moving to fintech)
samples.answer: From my FMCG experience, I know shopkeepers trust people who solve problems and come back. Before pitching, I would check what other payment QRs are already on the counter. If he has three, I would not ask him to remove them; I would show what extra benefit ours gives, such as [credit line for inventory, faster settlement, or loyalty features], if our company offers it. I would also mention that many shops on the same street have started using it, if that is true. Finally, I would leave my number and make sure his first settlement goes smoothly, because that one experience decides whether he recommends us.

mistakes: Pitching features in English jargon to a busy shopkeeper.
Hiding rental charges or terms.
Visiting during peak hours and insisting on attention.
Badmouthing competitor apps.
Promising loans or credit features that the company may not offer him.
follow_ups: He says he already has three QR codes. What now?
He is worried about charges. How do you respond?
How many merchants can you onboard in a day?
How would you get him to actually use the app after onboarding?
faqs: Do merchants pay charges on UPI?

Charges depend on the payment mode, the provider and current regulations. Person-to-merchant UPI has generally been free for most small merchants, but services like sound boxes may involve rental. Always check your company's current pricing and any NPCI or RBI updates.
Why do interviewers care about local language?

Small merchants often prefer their own language and trust people who speak it. Field sales success depends on rapport. Mentioning that you can pitch in the local language strengthens your answer considerably.

items.question: The customer says, 'I will think about it.' What do you do next?
items.title: Customer Says 'I'll Think About It': Sales Interview Answer
items.description: Handle the most common stalling objection in insurance, loan and investment sales: find the real concern, give space, and set a clear follow-up.
items.why_asked: 'I will think about it' is the most common way customers delay a decision, and it often hides a specific concern: price, trust, a spouse's opinion or not understanding the product. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can uncover the real objection politely, without pressuring the customer. They also want to see if you set a concrete next step instead of leaving the deal hanging. Pushy answers, such as creating fake urgency or saying the offer ends today when it does not, are red flags. Balanced answers respect the customer's need for time while keeping the conversation moving.
how_to_answer: Acknowledge the request respectfully, since buying financial products is an important decision and taking time is reasonable.
Ask a gentle question to uncover the concern, such as whether anything is unclear, or whether the premium or EMI feels high.
Address the specific concern if one comes up, with facts, a comparison or a smaller option.
Agree on a clear next step: a date and time to call, documents to share, or a meeting with the spouse or family.
Follow up as promised, and accept a final no gracefully if that is the answer.

samples.answer: I would say, 'Of course, sir, it is an important decision and you should be comfortable.' Then I would ask, 'Just so I can help you decide, is there any part that is not clear, or is it more about the premium?' Often the customer then tells me the real concern. If it is the premium, I could show a lower cover or a different payment frequency. If he wants to discuss with his wife, I would offer to explain it to both of them together. Before leaving, I would fix a time, like 'Shall I call you on Saturday at 11?' and send the brochure on WhatsApp. I would not say the offer ends today if it does not.

In home loans, customers often compare several lenders, so 'I will think about it' usually means they are waiting for another quote. I ask directly but politely whether they are comparing offers and what matters most to them, rate, processing fee or speed. Then I make sure they compare correctly, including fees and the reset terms of the floating rate. I give them a written summary of our offer and set a follow-up date. Some come back, some do not, but they remember that I was transparent.

mistakes: Creating false urgency, such as an offer that 'ends today' when it does not.
Leaving without a specific follow-up plan.
Repeating the whole pitch again instead of finding the concern.
Getting irritated or showing disappointment.
follow_ups: What if the customer does not pick up your follow-up call?
How many times would you follow up before stopping?
How do you handle 'your product is too expensive'?
What if the customer's spouse is against the purchase?
faqs: How many follow-ups are acceptable?

There is no fixed number, but two or three well-spaced, useful follow-ups are usually reasonable. Each should add something, like a clarification or document. If the customer clearly declines, stop and note it. Respecting a no protects your reputation.
Is creating urgency always wrong?
Real urgency is fine, such as a genuine offer deadline or the fact that insurance premiums rise with age. False urgency is misleading and can amount to mis-selling. Use only facts you can verify.

items.question: Can you bring business from your own network?
items.title: Can You Bring Business From Your Network? Sales Interview
items.description: Insurance, broking and NBFC sales interviewers ask about your network. Answer realistically, ethically and with a plan that goes beyond friends and family.
items.why_asked: Insurance agencies, broking firms, wealth desks and some NBFCs ask this because early business often comes from a salesperson's own contacts. The interviewer wants to estimate how quickly you can start producing and whether you understand ethical prospecting. They are also wary of candidates who overpromise, saying they will bring dozens of clients, and of those who would pressure relatives. A strong answer gives a realistic picture of your network, a respectful way to approach it, and, crucially, a plan to build new prospects after the warm market is exhausted.
how_to_answer: Be realistic about your network: describe the kinds of contacts you have, such as alumni, former colleagues, community groups or local businesses, without inflating numbers.
Explain how you would approach them respectfully, starting with understanding their needs and not pressuring anyone.
Mention that you would only offer products that genuinely suit them, since a bad sale to a relative damages both relationship and reputation.
Show a plan beyond your network: referrals, local events, workplace sessions, digital presence within compliance rules, and company leads.
Mention data and consent: using only contacts who are willing to hear from you, and following company rules on communication.

samples.answer: I have a reasonable network: my college alumni group, my father's colleagues and neighbours in our housing society. I would not want to approach them with a hard sell, though. My plan is to first share simple information about why term and health insurance matter, and let interested people come to me. A few people have already asked me about health insurance after a family member's hospitalisation. But I know my network alone will not sustain me for long. I would ask satisfied clients for referrals, hold small awareness sessions in our society and at local offices, and work the leads the company provides.

samples.who: Experienced (moving from a bank to a broking firm as RM)
samples.answer: Over [number] years at the bank I built relationships with many customers, but I want to be careful here. Those customers belong to the bank, and I cannot use its data. What I can bring is my professional reputation and contacts who know me personally, such as business owners I have stayed in touch with outside work. I would inform them that I have moved and let them choose. Beyond that, I plan to grow through referrals and investor education sessions. I expect it to take a few months to build a meaningful book.

mistakes: Promising a large number of clients you cannot deliver.
Planning to sell mainly to relatives under pressure.
Suggesting you will take client data from your previous employer.
Having no plan once your personal network is exhausted.
follow_ups: How many people do you think will buy from you in the first three months?
What will you do after approaching your network?
Can you use your previous employer's client list?
How would you ask for referrals?
faqs: Is it legal to contact my previous employer's clients?

Using your previous employer's client data or confidential lists can breach your employment agreement and data protection rules. You can inform personal contacts that you have moved, but check your agreement and avoid taking any client records. When in doubt, consult HR or legal.
What if I do not have a large network?

Say so honestly and focus on your plan to build one: company leads, referrals, community events and consistent follow-up. Many successful salespeople started without a network. Interviewers value a realistic plan more than a big claim.
